--- format: live-html: webr: packages: - survival --- # When proportional hazards fail {#sec-nonph} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## You need this chapter if… - `cox.zph()` flags your **main exposure** (treatment, say), not just a covariate; - the Kaplan–Meier curves **cross**, or come together and then separate; - you expect the effect to change over time: an operation with early risks and later benefits, or a test result that predicts the near future better than the distant one. If the problem is only with a covariate you're adjusting for, stratifying on it (@sec-ph-check) is usually enough. *This chapter builds on Chapter 3.* ::: ::: {.callout-note icon="false"} ## In this chapter **The question.** When the hazard ratio isn't constant, a single HR can be badly misleading. What should you report instead? **By the end of this chapter you will be able to:** - recognise when non-proportional hazards matter, and when they don't; - estimate a separate HR for each period of follow-up, and an HR that changes smoothly over time with `tt()`; - estimate and interpret the **restricted mean survival time (RMST)**, and explain why the choice of time horizon matters; - interpret an **accelerated failure time** model's time ratio. ::: ## First: does it matter? Chapter 3 showed how to check the proportional hazards assumption. Before changing your analysis, ask two questions. **Which variable fails?** If it's a covariate you're only adjusting for, **stratify** on it: each level gets its own baseline hazard, the variable gets no HR, and the HRs you care about are unaffected (Exercise 3.1 did this for ECOG). If a continuous covariate fails, split it into groups and stratify, or use the methods below. Problems with the **main exposure** need more thought, because they change what you can report. **How badly does it fail?** With a lot of data, `cox.zph()` can flag tiny, unimportant changes. Always look at the plot. If the line is roughly flat, with small wiggles, a single HR is a fair summary. If it clearly changes direction or size, a single HR misleads. ## A treatment whose effect reverses Here's a simulated trial where it matters. 800 patients are randomised to **surgery** or **medical treatment**. Surgery carries early risks: for the first 6 months the hazard of death is **twice** as high. After that, it's **half** as high. (The code is folded away; open it if you're interested.) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show the simulation code"} set.seed(2027) n <- 800 surgery <- rep(0:1, each = n / 2) # 400 medical (0), 400 surgery (1) u <- runif(n) h0 <- 0.4 # medical: constant hazard, 0.4 per year # Surgery: twice the hazard for 6 months, then half the hazard t_medical <- -log(u) / h0 t_surgery <- ifelse(-log(u) < 2 * h0 * 0.5, -log(u) / (2 * h0), 0.5 + (-log(u) - 2 * h0 * 0.5) / (0.5 * h0)) t_event <- ifelse(surgery == 1, t_surgery, t_medical) t_cens <- runif(n, 2, 5) # follow-up ends 2-5 years after entry trial <- data.frame( surgery = surgery, time = pmin(t_event, t_cens), status = as.numeric(t_event <= t_cens) ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ surgery, data = trial) |> ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) + add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") + scale_ggsurvfit() + labs(x = "Years") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Kaplan–Meier curves for the simulated trial. Surgery does worse at first, then better: the curves cross at about 1.8 years.](10-non-ph_files/figure-html/fig-nonph-km-1.png){#fig-nonph-km fig-align='center' width=770} ::: ::: The standard analysis: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ surgery, data = trial) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Call: #> survdiff(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ surgery, data = trial) #> #> N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V #> surgery=0 400 301 285 0.847 1.73 #> surgery=1 400 260 276 0.877 1.73 #> #> Chisq= 1.7 on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cox_naive <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ surgery, data = trial) summary(cox_naive)$conf.int ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95 #> surgery 0.8941873 1.118334 0.7570367 1.056185 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cox.zph(cox_naive) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> chisq df p #> surgery 46.8 1 7.7e-12 #> GLOBAL 46.8 1 7.7e-12 ``` ::: ::: The log-rank test (p = 0.2) and the Cox model (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.06) both say "no clear difference". That's badly misleading: surgery **doubles** the early hazard and **halves** the later one. The two effects cancel out in a single number. `cox.zph()` flags the problem strongly (p < 0.001). Here are the alternatives. ## Option 1: a separate HR for each period You met this in @sec-nonph-example. Split follow-up at a time chosen from the plot, or from clinical knowledge, and estimate an HR for each period: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} trial_split <- survSplit(Surv(time, status) ~ ., data = trial, cut = 0.5, episode = "period") trial_split$period <- factor(trial_split$period, levels = 1:2, labels = c("first 6 months", "after 6 months")) cox_period <- coxph(Surv(tstart, time, status) ~ surgery:period, data = trial_split) summary(cox_period)$conf.int ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95 #> surgery:periodfirst 6 months 2.2063576 0.4532357 1.6518444 2.9470172 #> surgery:periodafter 6 months 0.5245366 1.9064448 0.4211291 0.6533356 ``` ::: ::: In the first 6 months, surgery more than doubles the hazard (HR 2.21, 95% CI 1.65 to 2.95). After 6 months it halves it (HR 0.52, 0.42 to 0.65). Those are close to the true values we built in (2 and 0.5), and `cox.zph(cox_period)` shows no remaining problem. This is easy to explain, but it needs a sensible cut point, chosen **before** looking at p-values. ### Practice: a separate HR for each period *This is a live exercise: edit the code, click **Run Code**, and your answer is checked automatically. See @sec-live-exercises if you haven't used one before.* The simulated surgery `trial` is loaded. Split follow-up at **1 year** instead of 6 months, and estimate the surgery HR in each period. Replace each `______`, then click **Run Code**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_split'} ```{webr} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_split library(survival) set.seed(2027) n <- 800 surgery <- rep(0:1, each = n / 2) # 400 medical (0), 400 surgery (1) u <- runif(n) h0 <- 0.4 # medical: constant hazard, 0.4 per year # Surgery: twice the hazard for 6 months, then half the hazard t_medical <- -log(u) / h0 t_surgery <- ifelse(-log(u) < 2 * h0 * 0.5, -log(u) / (2 * h0), 0.5 + (-log(u) - 2 * h0 * 0.5) / (0.5 * h0)) t_event <- ifelse(surgery == 1, t_surgery, t_medical) t_cens <- runif(n, 2, 5) # follow-up ends 2-5 years after entry trial <- data.frame( surgery = surgery, time = pmin(t_event, t_cens), status = as.numeric(t_event <= t_cens) ) rm(n, surgery, u, h0, t_medical, t_surgery, t_event, t_cens) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_split' caption='Practice: a separate HR for each period'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_split #| caption: "Practice: a separate HR for each period" trial_split <- survSplit(Surv(time, status) ~ ., data = trial, cut = ______, episode = "period") trial_split$period <- factor(trial_split$period, levels = 1:2, labels = c("first year", "after 1 year")) cox_period <- coxph(Surv(______, time, status) ~ surgery:period, data = trial_split) summary(cox_period)$conf.int ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_split"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 1 Time is in years, so 1 year is `cut = 1`. ::: ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_split"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 2 After splitting, each row runs from `tstart` to `time`: `Surv(tstart, time, status)`. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_split"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```r trial_split <- survSplit(Surv(time, status) ~ ., data = trial, cut = 1, episode = "period") trial_split$period <- factor(trial_split$period, levels = 1:2, labels = c("first year", "after 1 year")) cox_period <- coxph(Surv(tstart, time, status) ~ surgery:period, data = trial_split) summary(cox_period)$conf.int ``` With the split at 1 year, the first period mixes the harmful first 6 months with 6 months of benefit, so its HR is smaller (about 1.4) than the true early HR of 2. The HR after 1 year (about 0.5) matches the true later effect. A cut point in the wrong place blurs the picture, which is why it should come from the plot or from clinical knowledge. ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_split' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_split #| check: true m <- .envir_result$cox_period if (!inherits(m, "coxph") || length(coef(m)) != 2) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Fit coxph(Surv(tstart, time, status) ~ surgery:period, data = trial_split).") } else if (!any(abs(.envir_result$trial_split$tstart - 1) < 1e-8)) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Split follow-up at 1 year: cut = 1.") } else { hr <- exp(coef(m)) list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct! HR %.2f in the first year and %.2f after it. The first-year HR mixes early harm with later benefit.", hr[1], hr[2])) } ``` ::: ## Option 2: an HR that changes smoothly over time Sometimes an effect fades gradually rather than switching at one moment. The `tt()` ("time transform") argument in `coxph()` lets the log-HR change with time, for example in proportion to log(time). The real `veteran` lung cancer trial is a classic example. The Karnofsky performance score strongly predicts survival, but `cox.zph()` shows its effect changes: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} vet <- survival::veteran cox.zph(coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ trt + karno, data = vet)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> chisq df p #> trt 0.307 1 0.57942 #> karno 11.959 1 0.00054 #> GLOBAL 13.577 2 0.00113 ``` ::: ::: So we let the Karnofsky effect change with log(time): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cox_tt <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ trt + karno + tt(karno), data = vet, tt = function(x, t, ...) x * log(t)) summary(cox_tt)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> coef exp(coef) se(coef) z Pr(>|z|) #> trt 0.02893722 1.0293600 0.189420215 0.1527673 8.785818e-01 #> karno -0.08314604 0.9202167 0.017168667 -4.8428945 1.279612e-06 #> tt(karno) 0.01323575 1.0133237 0.004337927 3.0511697 2.279517e-03 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## How to read this output - `karno` and `tt(karno)` together describe the effect of the score. The log-HR per point at time $t$ is `karno` + `tt(karno)` × log($t$). - `tt(karno)` is **positive** (p = 0.002), so the protective effect of a higher score gets weaker as time goes on. ::: The numbers are hard to read on their own, so calculate the HR at a few times, per 10 points of the score: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} b <- coef(cox_tt) days <- c(7, 30, 90, 180, 365) hr_10 <- exp(10 * (b["karno"] + b["tt(karno)"] * log(days))) data.frame(days = days, hr_per_10_points = round(hr_10, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> days hr_per_10_points #> 1 7 0.56 #> 2 30 0.68 #> 3 90 0.79 #> 4 180 0.87 #> 5 365 0.95 ``` ::: ::: A 10-point higher score goes with a 44% lower hazard in the first week (HR 0.56), but only a 5% lower hazard at a year (HR 0.95). That's the same story as `ph.karno` in Chapter 3: a doctor's rating of how well a patient is now predicts the near future much better than the distant future. The functional form (here log time) is a choice you make, so check it against the `cox.zph()` plot. The survival package's guide to time-dependent covariates [@survival_timedep] covers `tt()` in more detail. ## Option 3: the restricted mean survival time The **restricted mean survival time (RMST)** avoids hazards altogether. It is the **average survival time up to a chosen time horizon**, $\tau$ ("tau"). For example, "over the first 2 years, patients survived for 1.40 years on average". It equals the **area under the KM curve** up to $\tau$: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show the plotting code"} km_trial <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ surgery, data = trial) # Survival on a fine grid of times up to 2 years, for shading grid <- summary(km_trial, times = seq(0, 2, by = 0.005), extend = TRUE) stairs <- data.frame( time = grid$time, surv = grid$surv, arm = ifelse(grid$strata == "surgery=1", "Surgery", "Medical") ) ggplot(stairs, aes(time, surv, fill = arm, colour = arm)) + geom_area(alpha = 0.25, position = "identity") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + facet_wrap(~ arm) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#0072B2")) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#0072B2")) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2), ylim = c(0, 1)) + labs(x = "Years", y = "Survival probability") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The RMST up to 2 years is the shaded area under each KM curve. The difference in RMST is the difference between the two areas.](10-non-ph_files/figure-html/fig-rmst-area-1.png){#fig-rmst-area fig-align='center' width=770} ::: ::: The **survRM2** package compares two groups' RMSTs: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rmst_2y <- rmst2(time = trial$time, status = trial$status, arm = trial$surgery, tau = 2) rmst_2y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> The truncation time: tau = 2 was specified. #> #> Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) by arm #> Est. se lower .95 upper .95 #> RMST (arm=1) 1.256 0.041 1.176 1.336 #> RMST (arm=0) 1.404 0.035 1.336 1.472 #> #> #> Restricted Mean Time Lost (RMTL) by arm #> Est. se lower .95 upper .95 #> RMTL (arm=1) 0.744 0.041 0.664 0.824 #> RMTL (arm=0) 0.596 0.035 0.528 0.664 #> #> #> Between-group contrast #> Est. lower .95 upper .95 p #> RMST (arm=1)-(arm=0) -0.148 -0.252 -0.043 0.006 #> RMST (arm=1)/(arm=0) 0.895 0.826 0.969 0.006 #> RMTL (arm=1)/(arm=0) 1.248 1.068 1.459 0.005 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## How to read this output - **RMST** for each arm (`arm=1` is surgery, `arm=0` medical): the average survival time, in years, over the first 2 years, with a 95% CI. - **RMST (arm=1)-(arm=0)**: the difference. This is usually the number to report. - The ratio of RMSTs, and the RMTL rows (restricted mean time *lost*), are other ways of summarising the same thing. ::: Over the first 2 years, surgery patients survived on average 0.15 years (about 54 days) **less** than medical patients (95% CI 0.04 to 0.25 years less). But the answer depends on the horizon you choose: | Time horizon $\tau$ | RMST, medical | RMST, surgery | Difference (surgery − medical) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 year | 0.83 | 0.72 | −0.11 years | | 2 years | 1.40 | 1.26 | −0.15 years | | 4 years | 2.03 | 2.03 | 0.00 years | By 4 years, the later benefit of surgery has exactly made up for the early losses. All three answers are correct: they answer different questions. That's why $\tau$ must be **chosen in advance**, for a clinical reason (the length of time that matters to patients, or the follow-up most patients completed), and not picked afterwards to give the most interesting result. ### Interactive app: choosing the time horizon In this app you move $\tau$ and watch the RMSTs change. With the default settings, it uses exactly the trial above, so the numbers match the table. Changing the effect settings, or the seed, simulates a new trial. The bottom plot shows the RMST difference for **every** possible $\tau$, with your choice marked. ::: {.app} ```{ojs} //| echo: false import {simSwitch, rmst} from "./js/extras.js" import {kmFit} from "./js/survtools.js" formGrid = inputs => html`

On the **Default** scenario, move $\tau$ from 0.5 to 4.5 years. **Predict:** at what horizon does surgery stop looking worse? 2. **Predict:** what does the bottom plot look like if surgery has no early harm? *Then* pick **No early harm (HR 0.5 throughout)**. 3. **Predict:** if the later benefit is smaller, will surgery ever catch up within 4.5 years? *Then* pick **Smaller late benefit (HR 0.8)**, and then **Early harm lasts a year**. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"} ## Answers: what you should see 1. The difference starts negative (surgery patients lose time early: −0.11 years at 1 year and −0.15 at 2 years), shrinks (−0.09 at 3 years), and crosses zero at 4 years. By 4.5 years surgery is ahead (+0.07). The shaded areas show why: the early gap in the curves is eventually outweighed by the later one. This is why τ must be chosen in advance. 2. The difference is positive at every horizon, and grows steadily (+0.25 years at 2 years, +0.72 at 4). When hazards are proportional, the RMST and the HR tell the same story, and the choice of τ only changes the size of the benefit, not its direction. 3. **No.** With a later HR of 0.8, surgery never catches up within 4.5 years (−0.22 years at 4 years). If the early harm lasts a year, it doesn't either (−0.34 at 4 years). Whether surgery is "worth it" depends on how big and how long-lasting each effect is, and on the time horizon that matters to patients. ::: ### Practice: RMST at 3 years *This is a live exercise: edit the code, click **Run Code**, and your answer is checked automatically. See @sec-live-exercises if you haven't used one before.* Compare the two arms' RMSTs over the first **3 years**. The first run downloads the survRM2 package. Replace each `______`, then click **Run Code**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_rmst'} ```{webr} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_rmst if (!requireNamespace("survRM2", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("survRM2", quiet = TRUE) library(survRM2) library(survival) set.seed(2027) n <- 800 surgery <- rep(0:1, each = n / 2) # 400 medical (0), 400 surgery (1) u <- runif(n) h0 <- 0.4 # medical: constant hazard, 0.4 per year # Surgery: twice the hazard for 6 months, then half the hazard t_medical <- -log(u) / h0 t_surgery <- ifelse(-log(u) < 2 * h0 * 0.5, -log(u) / (2 * h0), 0.5 + (-log(u) - 2 * h0 * 0.5) / (0.5 * h0)) t_event <- ifelse(surgery == 1, t_surgery, t_medical) t_cens <- runif(n, 2, 5) # follow-up ends 2-5 years after entry trial <- data.frame( surgery = surgery, time = pmin(t_event, t_cens), status = as.numeric(t_event <= t_cens) ) rm(n, surgery, u, h0, t_medical, t_surgery, t_event, t_cens) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_rmst' caption='Practice: RMST at 3 years'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_rmst #| caption: "Practice: RMST at 3 years" rmst_3y <- rmst2(time = trial$time, status = trial$status, arm = trial$______, tau = ______) rmst_3y ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_rmst"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 1 The arm variable is `surgery`, and the horizon is `tau = 3` (years). ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_rmst"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```r rmst_3y <- rmst2(time = trial$time, status = trial$status, arm = trial$surgery, tau = 3) rmst_3y ``` Over the first 3 years, surgery patients survived on average 1.69 years, and medical patients 1.78 years: a difference of −0.09 years (95% CI −0.25 to 0.07). By 3 years the later benefit has made up most of the early losses, so the difference is small and not significant, between the 1- and 4-year results in the table above. ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_rmst' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_rmst #| check: true r <- .result if (!inherits(r, "rmst2")) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Make the last line the rmst2() result, rmst_3y.") } else if (r$tau != 3) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use a 3-year horizon: tau = 3.") } else { d <- r$unadjusted.result[1, 1] list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct! Difference in RMST over 3 years: %.2f years. The later benefit has made up most of the early losses.", d)) } ``` ::: ## Option 4: survival at fixed times The simplest absolute measure, from Chapter 2, also works whatever the hazards do: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} km_trial <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ surgery, data = trial) s <- summary(km_trial, times = c(0.5, 4)) data.frame(arm = s$strata, years = s$time, survival = round(s$surv, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> arm years survival #> 1 surgery=0 0.5 0.83 #> 2 surgery=0 4.0 0.20 #> 3 surgery=1 0.5 0.66 #> 4 surgery=1 4.0 0.31 ``` ::: ::: At 6 months, 83% of medical patients but only 66% of surgery patients were alive. At 4 years, it's 20% versus 31%. Reporting both, alongside the KM curves, tells the story clearly. ## Option 5: accelerated failure time models A different kind of regression model describes effects on **survival time** rather than on the hazard. An **accelerated failure time (AFT)** model estimates a **time ratio**: how many times longer (or shorter) one group's survival times are. `survreg()` in the survival package fits them. Here it is for sex in the `lung` data from Chapters 1–3: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lung <- survival::lung lung$status <- lung$status - 1 lung$sex <- factor(lung$sex, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Male", "Female")) aft <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung, dist = "weibull") exp(coef(aft))[2] # time ratio, women vs men ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> sexFemale #> 1.485242 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} exp(confint(aft))[2, ] # its 95% CI ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 2.5 % 97.5 % #> 1.156491 1.907447 ``` ::: ::: Women's survival times are about 1.49 times as long as men's (95% CI 1.16 to 1.91). Many people find "women lived about 50% longer" easier to grasp than "women had a 41% lower hazard". AFT models make their own assumption: that the time ratio is the same throughout follow-up, and that survival times follow the chosen distribution (here Weibull). So they're an *alternative* effect measure, not a cure for crossing curves like those in the surgery trial. ## Choosing an approach | Situation | Suggested approach | |---|---| | A covariate you're adjusting for fails PH | Stratify on it | | The effect switches at a clear time | A separate HR for each period | | The effect fades or grows gradually | `tt()`, checked against the `cox.zph()` plot | | You want one summary that doesn't depend on PH | RMST at a pre-specified $\tau$, plus survival at fixed times | | You'd like to describe effects on survival time | An AFT model (time ratio) | Whatever you choose, **show the KM curves**: they tell the reader what is happening, whichever summary you report alongside them. ## Quick quiz {.unnumbered} Choose an answer to each question. Problems with the **main exposure** change what you should report. - A single HR can hide **opposite effects** at different times, as in the surgery trial (HR 0.89 overall, but 2.2 early and 0.5 later). - A separate HR for each **period** (`survSplit()`) is easy to explain. `tt()` lets an effect change **smoothly** with time. - The **RMST** is the average survival time up to a horizon τ, the area under the KM curve. It doesn't rely on PH, but its answer depends on τ, so choose τ in advance. - **Survival at fixed times** and the **KM curves** themselves always help. - **AFT models** describe effects as **time ratios**, with their own assumptions. ::: **Answering the question.** Report what the data show over time: the KM curves, survival at clinically important times, and either period-specific HRs or the RMST at a horizon chosen in advance. In the surgery trial, these reveal early harm and later benefit, which the single HR of 0.89 hid completely. ## Further reading All of these are free to read online unless marked otherwise.
